title: Gender differences in cannabis use disorders: Results from the National Epidemiologic Survey of Alcohol and Related Conditions

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described mostly in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later; the general-population survey read here for alcohol did not find the full pattern; and in a US general-population survey of cannabis use disorder, read in full, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 0.40 years shorter in women, among people who already had the disorder and without adjustment for age, not the 2.5 years a critique reports. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among the 38,309 lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks ever), men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age). The authors read these hazards, the survival curves and a significant interaction of cohort, gender and time (its estimates not shown) as men becoming dependent faster, especially in younger cohorts. In the editors' reading, a hazard among all drinkers combines the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, and because the average times below were similar, the higher hazard in men mostly reflects that more men became dependent (in the table's unweighted counts, 23.7% of male and 16.2% of female lifetime drinkers; editors' arithmetic). Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted); it was shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years) and, not marked significant, in those born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4), and longer, not significantly, in women of the other three cohorts. Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the phrase 'telescoped development' was first used in 1958; the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term asked 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups to recall four landmark ages, and the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter on average in the women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Marks & Clark, 2018); read in full, the survey shows a much smaller difference, and the critique misreports both the difference and the sample. In NESARC 2001–2002 (43,093 US adults interviewed once, response 81%), the comparison was restricted to the 2,080 men and 1,217 women (3,297 in all) who had ever had DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence: they had first used cannabis at the same average age (16.71 against 16.73 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.34 against 18.98 years, not significant), and the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 2.64 years in men and 2.24 in women, a difference of 0.40 years, about 5 months (p = 0.026). The comparison was adjusted neither for current age, although the women with the disorder were younger, nor for anything else; it was one of about 50 comparisons made without correction (editors' count on the study card); and it describes speed among people who developed the disorder, not who develops it: the authors cite another analysis of the same survey in which 11.8% of men and 5.4% of women had ever had the disorder. The authors present the 0.40 years as evidence of telescoping outside treatment (Khan et al., 2013). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids, but not heroin, found mainly in women already in treatment, and, following an earlier review, explains the difference from population surveys by who is sampled: women in treatment likely have more severe disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; its cannabis citation points to a general-population paper on alcohol dependence). The same group's earlier review states as established that women advance faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies, among them treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996) that the review itself describes elsewhere as showing no earlier treatment entry for women (Greenfield et al., 2007). The treatment-sample study that the papers above describe in opposite ways, read in full, compared people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993, nine sites; 379 women and 1,210 men with all four landmark ages, recalled at entry; women and men compared within study arm and fifth of current age, nothing else adjusted for): women recalled first getting drunk regularly, first alcohol problems and first difficulty stopping drinking 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men (getting drunk regularly at 26.6 against 22.7 years on average) but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 against 35.0 years). The recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to the worst period (5.5 against 7.8 years), not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 against 2.2 years), and, among the 735 people for whom the trial was their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance; the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants (average age 26.6; getting drunk regularly at 18.8 against 18.0 years) and grew with age; and only 53% of participants reported the landmarks in the order the intervals assume. Women and men entered treatment at about the same ages (38 to 42 years on average), so a later start in women by itself shortens every interval that ends at treatment: women started getting drunk regularly 3.9 years later than men and reached first treatment 4.2 years sooner after that (editors' comparison), and in the editors' approximate reading of the paper's figure the gaps in time to treatment by age group (about 0.8 to 7.7 years) track the gaps in the age of getting drunk regularly (0.8 to 7.1 years). The authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment and recommend alerting women in general that they are more likely to develop alcohol problems rapidly (Randall et al., 1999); the papers that cite the study as showing telescoping, and the critique that counts it among studies with fewer telescoping effects, are each partly right. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks), men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed, read by the authors as faster progression in men; whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); share of lifetime drinkers with a time to dependence in the unweighted Table 1 counts, men 23.7% vs women 16.2% (4,631 of 19,549 and 3,121 of 19,263; editors' arithmetic; these counts total 7,752, against 8,564 people with dependence in the hazard analysis); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card), and longer in women in the other three cohorts (3.1 vs 2.8, 8.6 vs 7.9 and 11.8 vs 10.4 years; none marked significant); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): the 1989 study credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; 75 of 103 citing articles used the 1989 study as background. General-population survey of cannabis use disorder as described by Marks & Clark (2018): first use to the disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, in 1,217 women and 3,297 men; read in full (Khan et al., 2013; NESARC 2001–2002; 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence, 3,297 in all), men vs women, weighted means (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), p = 0.88; age at onset of the disorder 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), p = 0.10; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F = 5.20, p = 0.026, a difference of 0.40 years (approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72, editors' calculation on the study card), unadjusted, among people with the disorder; lifetime disorder in the whole survey, cited by the authors from another analysis, 11.8% of men vs 5.4% of women. Treatment sample, read in full (Randall et al., 1999; Project MATCH 1991–1993; 379 women, 1,210 men; compared within study arm and fifth of current age), women vs men, mean (SD) recalled age at getting drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96), first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87), loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95), worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93); intervals, drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67) years; drunk regularly to first treatment, 735 people in their first treatment (numbers of women and men not reported), 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67) years, F(1, 715) = 44.5; gender ω² .01 to .04; youngest fifth of current age, drunk regularly 18.8 vs 18.0 years, oldest fifth 37.8 vs 30.7.
